\section[\hi{मौसम}]{\hi{मौसम} — another Perso-Arabic loan, and a false-friend trap}

\label{lesson:HI-C20-mausam}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You've already seen Hindi borrow \emph{umr} from Arabic. Here's another one — and this time, English borrowed the SAME root too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{मौसम} — the same root as "monsoon"}
\textbf{\hi{मौसम}} (\emph{mausam}) = "\textbf{weather}" — borrowed from Classical \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{موسم}} (\emph{mawsim}), itself from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{مَوْسِم}} (\emph{mawsim}, "season, time of year, occasion"; likely originally used by Arab sailors for seasonal winds). This is the \textbf{exact same root} that gave English \textbf{monsoon} — carried into English in the \textbf{1580s}, well before the British Raj, via \textbf{Portuguese and Dutch} traders in the Indian Ocean spice trade (Portuguese \emph{monção}, Dutch \emph{monssoen}, both from this same Arabic \emph{mawsim}). So "monsoon" and Hindi's everyday word for "weather" are, quite directly, the same word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{गर्मी} \hi{है}, \hi{ठंड} \hi{है} — heat and cold, native words}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{गर्मी} \hi{है।}} — "It's hot." — literally "\textbf{there is heat}." (\emph{garmī hai.}) \textbf{\hi{ठंड} \hi{है।}} — "It's cold." — literally "\textbf{there is cold}." (\emph{ṭhanḍ hai.})
\end{quote}

Both use ordinary Hindi nouns (\textbf{\hi{गर्मी}}, "heat"; \textbf{\hi{ठंड}}, "cold") plus \textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}, "is/there is") — simpler in shape than Arabic's fully verbless pattern, since Hindi still needs \emph{hai} here.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{बारिश} vs. \hi{वर्षा} — a genuine false-friend trap}
Hindi has \textbf{two} words for "rain" that sound similar enough to assume they're related — \textbf{don't} make that assumption:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{बारिश}} (\emph{baarish}) — from \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{بارش}} (\emph{bāriš}) — the everyday, colloquial word: \textbf{\hi{बारिश} \hi{हो} \hi{रही} \hi{है}} ("it's raining," literally "rain is happening").
  \item \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} (\emph{varṣā}) — fully \textbf{native Sanskrit}, from \textbf{\hi{वर्ष}} (\emph{varṣá}, "rain"), tracing to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}wers-}} ("to rain") — cousin of Greek \textbf{hérsē} ("dew") and Old Irish \textbf{frass} ("rain-shower"). This is the more formal/literary word.
\end{itemize}

Despite the similar sound, dictionaries flag \emph{baarish} and \emph{varṣā} as \textbf{probably not related} — one's a Persian loan, the other a native Sanskrit inheritance from deep in the Indo-European family. A likely false-friend trap, not a confirmed doublet.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "mausam" — weather, same root as English "monsoon"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "garmī hai. ṭhanḍ hai." — it's hot / it's cold{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "baarish hai" (everyday) vs. "varṣā" (formal) — probably NOT related despite sounding alike{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What English word shares \hi{मौसम}'s exact root, and how did it reach English? (\textbf{Monsoon} — from Arabic \emph{mawsim} via Persian, carried into English in the 1580s by Portuguese/Dutch traders, well before the British Raj.) Are \textbf{\hi{बारिश}} and \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} related words? (\textbf{Probably not} — despite sounding similar, \emph{baarish} is a Persian loan and \emph{varṣā} is native Sanskrit; dictionaries flag them as likely unrelated.) What PIE root does \textbf{\hi{वर्षा}} trace to, and what's its Greek cousin? (\emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}wers-}}, "to rain" — cousin of Greek \emph{hérsē}, "dew.")
\end{tcolorbox}
